summary: A revised draft table of contents for the Internet Protocol Handbook, a planned collection of the main internet protocol documents. It takes the place of the earlier draft contents list in RFC 766.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC lists the planned contents of an Internet Protocol Handbook. It groups existing protocol documents by their role and includes appendices.

subtitle: A draft table of contents for a planned Internet Protocol Handbook.

tldr.problem: As Internet protocols replaced older ARPANET protocols, readers needed a planned collection of the related RFCs and IENs.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 774 publishes a draft table of contents grouped into overview, gateway, host, application and appendix sections.
tldr.outcome: It replaces the draft contents in RFC 766 and is a handbook outline, not a protocol specification.

today: RFC 774 obsoletes RFC 766. It is a draft contents list for a planned handbook, not a protocol specification.

sections.title: The Planned Handbook
sections.content:
The Internet Protocol Handbook was planned by the Network Information Center as the Internet family of protocols replaced the old ARPANET protocols. The RFC says the handbook was tentatively planned to be available at the end of 1980.

It was intended to parallel the ARPANET Protocol Handbook and primarily collect existing RFCs and IENs. RFC 774 replaces the earlier draft table of contents in RFC 766.
sections.plainLanguage: The handbook was planned as a collection of existing RFCs and IENs. This memo gives a draft list of its contents.

sections.title: How the Contents Are Grouped
sections.content:
The draft table of contents has sections for Overview, Gateway Level, Host Level, Application Level and Appendices. Gateway and host entries include documents on Internet Protocol, User Datagram Protocol and Transmission Control Protocol.

The application section includes entries for time service, name service, trivial file transfer, Telnet, file transfer, mail transfer and Internet Message Protocol. The appendices list assigned numbers, address mappings, document file format standards and mail header format standards.
sections.plainLanguage: The outline moves from an overview to gateway and host protocols, then applications and appendices. It lists document titles with RFC or IEN identifiers.

sections.title: Finding the Listed Documents
sections.content:
The memo says RFCs and IENs are public-access document files that can be copied from the Network Information Center's online Library at SRI-KL using FTP with the user name ANONYMOUS and password GUEST.

IEN file pathnames include a hyphen before the number, while RFC pathnames do not. The RFC points out this naming inconsistency.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo gives an FTP location and account details for retrieving the listed documents. It notes a difference in the IEN and RFC filename patterns.
